items: British Overseas Territory in the Indian Ocean
Atoll in the Chagos Archipelago, Indian Ocean
books:
The British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) is a British Overseas Territory situated in the Indian Ocean. The territory comprises the seven atolls of the Chagos Archipelago with over 1,000 individual islands, many very small, amounting to a total land area of 60 square kilometres (23 square miles). The largest and most southerly island is Diego Garcia, 27 square kilometres (10 square miles), the site of a Joint Military Facility of the United Kingdom and the United States. Official administration is remote from London, though the local capital is often regarded as being on Diego Garcia.
Mauritius claims that the British government separated the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius, creating a new colony, the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT). There are ongoing negotiations on this dispute.

Since 1971, only personnel of the British and United States military and associated contractors have been legally allowed to live on the Chagos Islands. The forced removal of Chagossians from the Chagos Archipelago occurred between 1968 and 1973. The Chagossians, then numbering about 2,000 people, were expelled by the British government to Mauritius and Seychelles, even from the outlying islands far away from the military base on Diego Garcia. Despite calls from numerous human rights organisations, the British government has repeatedly denied Chagossians the right of return. In 2026, six Chagossians returned to Île du Coin in an attempt to reestablish a permanent settlement, without seeking government permission; their effort is being challenged in court. In March 2026, the BIOT Supreme Court ruled that the Chagossians had the right to live on the island, but the territorial administration is appealing the ruling.

Since the 1980s, the Government of Mauritius has sought to gain control over the Chagos Archipelago, which was separated from the then Crown Colony of Mauritius by the UK in 1965 to form the British Indian Ocean Territory.

Diego Garcia (/diˈeɪ.ɡoʊ ɡɑːrˈsiːə/) is a coral atoll in the central Indian Ocean, the largest and southernmost of the atolls of the Chagos Archipelago. Its nearly continuous, V-shaped rim of land, about 64 kilometres (40 mi) long, almost encloses a lagoon of 124 square kilometres (48 sq mi) and holds more than half of the archipelago's land. Administered by the United Kingdom as part of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT), and claimed by Mauritius, it is the site of a joint British–American military base, Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia; it has no permanent inhabitants, and around 2,000 military personnel, officials and contractors are ordinarily present.

Known to Portuguese navigators from the early 16th century and claimed by France from 1769, the atoll was settled from the 1780s by planters from Île de France (Mauritius) with enslaved workers brought mainly from Madagascar and Mozambique. It passed to Britain with Mauritius in 1810–1814, and for 150 years its plantations at East Point, Pointe Marianne and Minni Minni produced coconut oil and copra; it was briefly a coaling station in the 1880s and a flying-boat base in the Second World War. The descendants of the plantation workers formed a community known as the Ilois, now generally called Chagossians.

In 1965 the United Kingdom detached the archipelago from Mauritius to form the BIOT and, under the 1966 UK–US exchange of notes, made it available for the defence purposes of both governments. The inhabitants of Diego Garcia were removed in 1971, and the rest of the archipelago was emptied by 1973 (see Expulsion of the Chagossians). An American naval communications station built from 1971 was expanded under the Diego Garcia Agreement 1976 into a naval support facility, which has since been used for operations in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan; in 2008 the British government acknowledged that the island had been used for two American extraordinary rendition flights in 2002.
